script.text: Racism is not the issue at stake.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: One should never miss an occasion to denounce it.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: None of us are in favor of racism. You're obscuring the issue, it's simply a question of a cat being run over by a pachyderm–in this case, a rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I'm a Northerner myself. Southerners have got too much imagination, Perhaps it was merely a flea run over by a mouse. People make mountains out of molehills.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to DUDARD) Let’s try and get things straight. Did you yourself, with your own eyes, see a rhinoceros strolling through the streets of the town?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It didn't stroll, it ran.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, I didn't see it personally. But a lot of very reliable people!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (interrupting him) It's obvious they were just making it up. You put too much trust in these journalists; they don't care what they invent to sell their wretched newspapers and please the bosses they serve!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: And you mean to tell me they've taken you in--you, a qualified man of law! Forgive me for laughing! Ha! Ha! Ha!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: But I saw it, I saw the rhinoceros. I'd take my oath on it.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: And I thought you were a sensible girl!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Mr. Botard, I can see straight! And I wasn't the only one, there were plenty of other people watching.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Pfff! They were probably watching something else! A few idlers with nothing to do, unemployed loiterers!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It happened yesterday, Sunday.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I work on Sundays as well. I've no time for priests who do their utmost to get you to church, just to prevent you from working and earning your daily bread by the sweat of your brow.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (indignant) Oh!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to offend you. The fact that I despise religion doesn't mean I don't esteem it highly. (To DAISY:) In anycase, do you know what a rhinoceros looks like?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It's a… it's a very big, ugly animal.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: And you pride yourself on your precise thinking! The rhinoceros, my dear young lady . . .

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: There's no need to start a lecture on the rhinoceros here. We' re not in school.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: That's a pity.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: During these last speeches BERENGER is seen climbing the last steps of the staircase; he opens the office door cautiously; as he does so one can read the notice on it: 'Editions de Droit'

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Well! It's gone nine, Miss Daisy, put the time sheets away. Too bad about the late-comers. .

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY goes to the little table, left, on which the time sheets are placed, at the same moment as BERENGER enters.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: entering, whilst the others continue their discussion, to DAISY

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Good morning, Miss

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'm not late, am I?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD and PAPILLON) I campaign against ignorance wherever I find it . . . !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BERENGER) Hurry up, Mr. Berenger.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: .. in palace or humble hut!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BERENGER) Quick! Sign the time sheet!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: : Oh thank you! Has the Boss arrived?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (a finger on her lips) Shh ! Yes, he's here.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Here already? (He tries to sign the time sheet.)

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (continuing) No matter where! Even in printing offices.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to BOTARD) Mr. Botard, I consider ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (signing the sheet, to DAISY) But it's not ten past ...

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to BOTARD) I consider you have gone too far.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to PAPILLON) I think so too, sir.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to BOTARD) Are you suggesting that Mr. Dudard, my colleague and yours, a law graduate and a first-class employee, is ignorant?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I wouldn't go so far as to say that, but the teaching you get at the university isn't up to.what you get at the ordinary schools.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to DAISY) What about that time sheet?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to PAPILLON) Here it is, sir. (She hands it to him.)

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD) There's no clear thinking at the universities, no encouragement for practical observation.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BorARD) Oh come now!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to PAPILLON) Good morning, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He has been making his way to the coat-rack behind the Chief’s back and around the group formed by the three characters; there he takes down his working overall or his well-worn coat, and hangs up his street coat in its place; he changes his coat by the coat-rack, then makes his way to his desk, from the drawer of which he takes out his black protective sleeves, etc.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Morning, Mr. Papillon ! Sorry I was almost late. Morning Dudard ! Morning, Mr. Botard.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Well Berenger, did you see the rhinoceros by any chance?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD) All you get at the universities are pretentious intellectuals with no practical knowledge of life.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BOTARD) Rubbish!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: continuing to arrange his working equipment with excessive zeal as if to make up for his late arrival; in a natural tone to PAPILLON

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh yes, I saw it all right.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (turning round) Pfff!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: So you see, I'm not mad after all.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (ironic) Oh, Mr. Berenger says that out of chivalry— he's a very chivalrous man even if he doesn't look it.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What’s chivalrous about saying you've seen a rhinoceros?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: A lot–when it's said to bolster up a fantastic statement by Miss Daisy. Everybody is chivalrous to Miss Daisy, it's very understandable.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Don't twist the facts, Mr. Botard. Mr. Berenger took no part in the argument. He's only just arrived.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DAISY) But you did see it, didn't you? We both did.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Pfff! It's possible that Mr. Berenger thought he saw a rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He-makes a·sign behind BERENGER’S back to indicate he drinks.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: He's got such a vivid imagination! Anything's possible with him!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I wasn't alone when I saw the rhinoceros! Or perhaps there were two rhinoceroses.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: He doesn't even know how many he saw!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I was with my friend Jean! And other people were there, too.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to BERENGER) I don't think you know what you're talking about.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It was a unicorned rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Pff ! They're in league, the two of them, to have us on.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to DAISY) I rather think it had two horns, from what I've heard!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: You'd better make up your minds.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (looking at the time) That will do, gentlemen, time's getting on.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Did you see· one rhinoceros, Mr. Berenger, or two rhinoceroses?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well, it's hard to say!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: You don't know. Miss Daisy saw one unicorned rhinoceros. What about your rhinoceros, Mr. Berenger, if indeed there was one, did it have one horn or two?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Exactly, that's the whole problem.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: And it's all very dubious.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Oh!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I don't mean to be offensive. But I don't believe a word of it. No rhinoceros has ever been seen in this country!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: There's a first time for everything.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: It has never been seen! Except in school-book illustrations. Your rhinoceros is a myth!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: A myth?

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Gentlemen I think it is high time we started to work.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DAISY) A myth– like flying saucers.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: But nevertheless a cat was trampled to death– that you can't deny.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I was a witness to that.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (pointing to BERENGER) In front of witnesses.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Yes, and what a witness!

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Gentlemen, gentlemen!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD) An example of collective psychosis, Mr. Dudard. Just like religion– the opiate of the people !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Well I believe flying saucers exist!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Pfff !

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (firmly) That's quite enough. There's been enough gossip! Rhinoceros or no rhinoceros, saucers or no saucers, work must go on! You're not paid to waste your time arguing about real or imaginary animals.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Imaginary!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Real!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Very real!

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Gentlemen,I remind you once again that we are in working hours. I am putting an end to this futile discussion.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (wounded and ironic) Very well, Mr. Papillon. You are the Chief. Your wishes are our commands.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Get on, gentlemen. I don't want to be forced to make a deduction from your salaries ! Mr. Dudard, how·is your report on the·alcoholic repression law coming along?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I'm just finishing it off, sir.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Then do so. It's very urgent. Mr. Berenger and Mr. Botard, have you finished correcting the proofs for the wine trade control regulations?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Not yet, Mr. Papillon. But they're well on the way.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Then finish off the corrections together. The printers are waiting. And Miss Daisy, you bring the letters to my office for signature. Hurry up and get them typed.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Very good, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY goes and types at her little desk. DUDARD sits at his desk and starts·to work. BERENGER and BOTARD sit at their little tables in profile to the auditorium. BOTARD, his back to the staircase, seems in a bad temper, BERENGER is passive and limp; he spreads the proofs on the table, passes the manuscript to BOTARD; BOTARD sits down grumbling, whilst PAPILLON exits banging the door loudly.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: I shall see you shortly, gentlemen. (Goes out.)

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: reading and correcting whilst BOTARD checks the manuscript with a pencil

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Laws relating to the proprietary control of wine produce… (he corrects) control with one L… (he corrects) Proprietary. One P, proprietary…the controlled wines of the Bordeaux region, the lower section of the upper slopes …

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I haven't got that! You've skipped a line.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'll start again. The Wine Control!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BERENGER and BOTARD) Please don't read so loud. I can't concentrate with you shouting at the tops of your voices.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD, over BERENGER's head, resuming the recent discussion, whilst BERENGER continues the corrections on his own for a few moments; he moves his lips noiselessly as he reads)

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: It's all a hoax.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What's all a hoax?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Your rhinoceros business, of course. You've been making all this propaganda to get these rumours started!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (interrupting his work) What propaganda?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (breaking in) No question of any propaganda.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (interrupting her typing) Do I have to tell you again, I saw it. I actually saw it, and others did, too.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BOTARD) You make me laugh! Propaganda! Propaganda for what?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD) Oh you know more about that than I do. Don't make out you're so innocent.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (getting angry) At any rate, Mr. Botard, I'm not in the pay of any furtive underground organization.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: That's an insult, I'm not standing for that …· (Rises)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pleading) Now, now, Mr. Botard…

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to DUDARD, who has also risen) Now, now, Mr. Dudard ...

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I tell you it's an insult.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: MR. PAPILLON's door suddenly opens. BOTARD and DUDARD. sit down again quickly; MR. PAPILLON is holding the time sheet in his hand; there is silence at his appearance.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Is Mr. Boeuf not in today?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (looking around) No, he isn’t. He must be absent.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Just when I needed him. (to DAISY) Did he let anyone know he was ill or couldn’t come in?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: He didn’t say anything to me.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (Opening his door wide and coming in) If this goes on I shall fire him. It's not the first time he's played me this trick. Up to now I haven't said anything, but it's not going on like this. Has anyone got the key to his desk?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: At this moment MRS. BOEUF enters. She has been seen during the last speech coming up the stairs. She bursts through the door, out of breath, apprehensive.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh here's Mrs. Boeuf

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Morning, Mrs. Boeuf.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: Morning, Mr. Papillon. Good morning everyone.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Well, where's your husband? What's happened to him? Is it too much trouble for him to show up to work anymore?

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (breathless) Please excuse him, my husband I mean... he went to visit his family for the weekend. He's got a touch of flu.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: So he's got a touch of flu, has he?

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (handing a paper to PAPILLON) He says so in the telegram. He hopes to be back on Wednesday. (Almost fainting.) Could I have a glass of water ... and sit down a moment…

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER takes his own chair center stage, on which she flops.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to DAISY) Give her a glass of water.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, straightaway!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She goes to get her a glass of water, and gives it to her during the following speeches.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to PAPILLON) She must have a weak heart.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: It's a great nuisance that Mr. Boeuf can't come. But that's no reason for you to go to pieces.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (with difficulty) It's not…it's…well I was chased here all the way from the house by a rhinoceros…

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How many horns did it have?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (guffawing) Don't make me laugh!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (indignant) Give her a chance to speak!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: making a great effort to be exact, and pointing in the direction of the staircase

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: It's down there, by the entrance. It seemed to want to come upstairs. At this moment a noise is heard. The staircase steps are seen to crumble under an obviously formidable weight. From below an anguished trumpeting is heard.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: As the dust clears after the collapse of the staircase, the staircase landing is seen to be hanging in space.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: My God!

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (seated, her hand on her heart) Oh! Ah!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER runs to·adminster to MRS. BOEUF, patting her cheeks and making her drink.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Keep calm!. .

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: Meanwhile PAPILLON, DUDARD and BOTARD rush left,jostling each other in their efforts to open the door, and stand covered in dust on the landing; the trumpetings continue to be heard.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to MRS. BOEUF) Are you feeling better now, Mrs. Boeuf?

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (on the landing) There it is! Down there! It is one!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I don’t see anything.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Of course it's one, down there, turning round and round. It can't get up here. There's no staircase any longer.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: It's most strange. What can it mean?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (turning towards BERENGER) Come and look. Come and have a look at your rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm coming.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER rushes to the landing, followed by DAISY who abandons MRS. BOEUF.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to BERENGER) You're the rhinoceros expert– take a good look.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm no rhinoceros expert . . . .

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Oh look at the way it's going round and round. It looks as if it was in pain…what can it want?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It seems to be looking for someone. (To BOTARD) Can you see it now?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (vexed) Yes, yes, I can see it.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to BERENGER) It's obviously a rhinoceros, That's what you saw before, isn't it? (To

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: ) And you, too?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Definitely.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's got two horns. It's an African rhinoceros, or Asian rather. Oh! I don't know whether the African rhinoceros has one horn or two.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: It's demolished the staircase-and a good thing, too! When you think how long I've been asking the management to install stone steps in place of that worm-eaten old staircase.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I sent a report a week ago, Chief

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: It was bound to happen, I.knew that. I could see it coming, and I was right.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to PAPILLON, ironically) As always.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DUDARD and PAPILLON) Now look, are two horns a characteristic of the Asian rhinoceros or the African?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Poor thing, it keeps on trumpeting and going round and round. What does it want? Oh, it's looking at us! (To the rhinoceros.) Kitty, kitty, kitty ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I shouldn't try to pet it, it's probably not tame ...

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: In any case, it's out of reach.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The rhinoceros gives a horrible trumpeting.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Poor thing!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: How can it be possible in a civilized country?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BOTARD) All right. But does it exist or not?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: It's all a classic conspiracy!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: With a political orator's gesture he points to DUDARD, quelling·him with a look.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: It's all your fault!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Why mine, rather than yours?

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: Ah! Oh!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (furious) Mine?

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: We're in a fine mess with no staircase.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BOTARD and DUDARD) Calm down, this is no time to argue!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: Meanwhile the rhinoceros has continued its trumpeting. MRS. BOEUF has risen and joined the group. For a few moments she stares fixedly at the rhinoceros turning round and round below; suddenly she lets out a terrible cry.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: My God! It can't be true!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to MRS. BOEUF) What’s the matter?

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: It's my husband. Oh Boeuf, my poor Boeuf, what's happened to you? .

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to MRS. BOEUF) Are you positive?

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: l recognize him, I recognize him!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The rhinoceros replies with a violent but tender trumpeting.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Well! That's the last straw. This time he's fired for good!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (aside) I understand it all now ...

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (fainting into BERENGER's arms) Oh! My God!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Carry her over here!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER, helped by DUDARD and DAISY, installs MRS. BOEUF in a chair.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (while they are carrying her) Don’t upset yourself, Mrs. Boeuf.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: Ah! Oh!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Maybe it can all be put right. . .!

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to DUDARD) Legally, what can be done? Can we collect insurance?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to PAPILLON) Is he insured?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: How can you talk about insurance at a time like this?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to PAPILLON) You need a lawyer’s advice.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (following the procession, raising his hands to heaven) It's pure madness ! What a society !

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: They crowd around MRS. BOEUF, pinching her cheeks; she opens her eyes, emits an 'Ah' and closes them again; they continue to. pinch her cheeks as BOTARD speaks

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: You can be certain of one thing: I’m reporting this to my union.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (coming to) My poor darling, I can't leave him like that, my poor darling. (A trumpeting is heard.) He's calling me. (Tenderly) He's calling me.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Feeling better now, Mrs. Boeuf?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: She's picking up·a bit.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to MRS. BOEUF) You can count on the union’s support. I won’t let this be hushed up.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Work's going to be delayed again. What about the post, Miss Daisy?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: First I want to know how we're going to get out of here.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: It is a problem. Through the window.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: They all go to the window with the exception of MRS. BOEUF slumped in her chair, and BOTARD, who stays center stage.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (at window) It's too high.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps we ought to call the firemen, and get them to bring ladders! .

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Miss Daisy; go to my office and telephone the fire brigade. (He follows her.)

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY goes out up-stage and one hears her voice on the telephone say: 'Hello, hello, is that the Fire Brigade?' followed by a vague sound of telephone conversation.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: (rising suddenly) I can't desert him, I can't desert him now!

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: If you want to divorce him you'd be perfectly justified.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You'd be the injured party.

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: No! Poor thing! This is not the moment for that. I won't abandon my husband in such a state.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: You're a good woman._

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to MRS. BOEUF) But what are you going to do?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She runs left towards the landing.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Watch out!

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: I can't leave him, I can't leave him now!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Hold her back!

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: I'm taking him home.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: What's she trying to do?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: preparing to jump; on the edge of the landing

script.speaker: Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: I'm coming my darling, I'm coming!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: She's going to jump.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: It's no more than her duty.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: She can't do that.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: Everyone with the exception of DAISY who is still telephoning, is near MRS. BOEUF on the landing; she jumps. BERENGER who tries to restrain her, is left with her skirt in his hand.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I couldn't hold her back.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The rhinoceros is heard from below, tenderly trumpeting.

script.speaker: Voice Of Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: Here I am, my sweet, I'm here now.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: She landed on his back in the saddle.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: She's a good rider.

script.speaker: Voice Of Mrs. Boeuf
script.text: Home now, dear, let's go home.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: They're off at a gallop.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DUDARD, BOTARD, BERENGER, PAPILLON come back onstage and go to the window.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're moving fast.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to PAPILLON) Ever done any riding?

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: A bit… a long time ago. (turning to the upstage door, to DUDARD) Is she still on the telephone?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (following the path of the rhinoceros) They're already a long way off. They’re out of sight.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (coming on stage) I had trouble getting the firemen.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (as if concluding an interior monologue) A fine state of affairs!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I had trouble getting the firemen!

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Are there fires all over the place, then?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I agree with Mr. Botard. Mrs. Boeuf's attitude is very moving; she's a woman of feeling.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: It means one employee less, who has to be replaced.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you really think he's no use to us any more?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: No, there aren't any fires, the firemen: have been called out for other rhinoceroses.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: For other rhinoceroses?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, other rhinoceroses. They've been reported all over the town. This morning there were seven, now there are seventeen.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: What did I tell you?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: As many as thirty-two have been reported. They're not official yet, but they're bound to be confirmed soon.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (less certain) Pff! ! They always exaggerate.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Are they coming to get us out of here?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm hungry!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, they're coming; the firemen are on the way.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: What about the work? We'll have to make up for the lost time.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well, Mr. Botard, do you still deny all rhinocerotic evidence?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD) No, Mr. Dudard, I do not deny the rhinocerotic evidence. I never have.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That's not true.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Oh no, that's not true.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I repeat I have never denied it. I just want to find out exactly where it is all leading. Because I know my own mind. I'm not content to simply state that a phenomenon exists. I make it my business to understand it before I explain it.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Then explain it to us.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, explain it, Mr. Botard.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Explain it, when your colleagues ask you.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I will explain it…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: We're all listening.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'm most curious.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I will explain it…one day…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Why not now?

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (menacingly, to MR. PAPILLON) We'll go into the explanation later, in private. (To everyone) I know the whys and the wherefores of this whole business…

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: What whys?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What wherefores?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I'd give a lot to know these whys and wherefores…

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (continuing; with a terrible air) And I also know the names of those responsible. The names of the traitors. You can't fool me. I'll let you know the purpose and the meaning of this whole plot ! I'll unmask the perpetrators!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But who'd want to…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BOTARD) You're evading the question, Mr. Botard.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: Let's have no evasions.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Evading? What, me?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Just now, yes.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: It's an open secret, gentlemen.-Even the man in the street knows about it. Only hypocrites pretend not to understand. The noise and hooting of a fire-engine is heard. The brakes are abruptly applied just under the window.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: That's the firemen!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: There’s going to be some big changes made. They won’t get away with this as easily as that.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That doesn't mean anything, Mr. Botard. The rhinoceroses exist, and that's that. That's all there is to it.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (at the window, looking down) Up here, firemen!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: A bustling is heard below, commotion, engine noises.

script.speaker: Voice Of Fireman
script.text: Put up the ladder!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (to DUDARD) I hold the key to all these happenings, using an infallible system of interpretation.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: I want you all back in the office this afternoon.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The firemen's ladder is placed against the window.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Too bad about the office, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: I don't know what the management will say!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: These are exceptional circumstances.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: They can't force us to come back this way! We’ll have to wait until the staircase is repaired.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: If anyone breaks a leg, it'll be the management's responsibility.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: That's true.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: A fireman's helmet is seen followed by the fireman.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DAISY pointing to the window) After you, Miss Daisy.

script.speaker: Fireman
script.text: Come on, Miss.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The fireman takes DAISY in his arms; she steps into the window and disappears with him.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Good-bye Miss Daisy. See you soon.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (disappearing) See you soon, good-bye!

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (at window) Telephone me tomorrow morning, Miss Daisy. You can come and type the letters at my house. (To BERENGER) Mr. Berenger, I draw your attention to the fact that we are not on holiday, and that work will resume as soon as possible.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (To the other two) You hear what I say, gentlemen?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Of course, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Fireman
script.text: (reappearing at window) Who's next?

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to all three of themJ Go on!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: After you, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: After you, Chief.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: You first, of course.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to BERENGER) Bring me Miss Daisy's letters. There, on the table.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER goes and gets the letters, brings them to PAPILLON.

script.speaker: Fireman
script.text: Come on, hurry up. We've not got all day. We've got other calls to make.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: PAPILLON, the letters under his arm, steps astride the window.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (to the FIREMAN) Careful of the documents! (Turning to the others) Good-bye, gentlemen.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Good-bye, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Goodbye, Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Papillon
script.text: (he has disappeared; we hear him say) Careful of my papers. Dudard! Lock up the offices!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (shouting) Don't you worry, Mr. Papillon. (To BOTARD) After you, Mr. Botard.

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: I am about to descend, gentlemen. And I am going to take this matter up immediately with the proper authorities. I'll get to the bottom of this so-called mystery. (He moves to window.)

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BOTARD) I thought it was all perfectly clear to you!

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (astride the window) Your irony doesn't affect me. What I'm after are the proofs and· the documents-–yes, proof positive of your treason.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That's absurd…

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: Your insults…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (interrupting him) It's you who are insulting me ...

script.speaker: Botard
script.text: (disappearing) I don't insult. I merely prove.

script.speaker: Voice Of Fireman
script.text: Come on there !

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BERENGER) What are you doing this afternoon? Shall we meet for a drink?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Sorry, I can't. I'm taking advantage of this afternoon off to go and see my friend Jean. I do want to make it up with him, after all. We got carried away. It was all my fault.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The fireman's head reappears at the window.

script.speaker: Fireman
script.text: Come along there!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pointing to the window) After you.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: After you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh no, after you.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, I insist, after you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No, please, after you, after you.

script.speaker: Fireman
script.text: Hurry up!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: After you, after you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No, after you, after·you. e They climb through the window together. The fireman helps them down, as the curtain falls.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: END OF ACT TWO, SCENE ONE.
ACT TWO SCENE TWO: CHEZ JEAN

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN's house. The layout is roughly the same as Act Two, Scene One. That is to say, the stage is divided into two. To the right, occupying three-quarters or four-fifths of the stage, according to size, is JEAN'S bedroom. Up-stage, a chair or an armchair, on which BERENGER will sit. Right centre, a door leading to JEAN's bathroom. When JEAN goes in to wash, the noise of a faucet is heard, and that of the shower. To the left of the room, a partition divides the stage in two. Center stage, the door leading to the stairs is less realistic, more stylized decor is preferred, the door. may be placed without a partition. To the left is the staircase; the top steps are visible, leading to JEAN's flat, the banister and the landing. At the back, on the landing level, is the door to the neighbour's flat. Lower down, at the back, there is a glass door, over which is written: 'Concierge'.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: When the curtain rises, JEAN is in bed, lying under the blanket, his back to the audience. One hears him cough. After a few moments BERENGER is seen, climbing the top steps of the staircase. He knocks at the door; JEAN does not answer. BERENGER knocks again.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Jean! (He knocks again.) Jean! The door at the end of the landing opens slightly, and a little old man with a white goatee appears.

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: What is it?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I want to see Jean. I am a friend of his.

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: I thought it was me you wanted. My name's Jean as well, but it's the other one you want.

script.speaker: Voice Of Old Man's Wife
script.text: (from within the room) Is it for us?

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: (turning to his wife who is not seen) No, for the other one.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (knocking) Jean!

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: I didn't see him go out. But I saw him last night. He looked terrible.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, I know why; it was my fault.

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: Perhaps he doesn't feel like opening the door to you. Try again.

script.speaker: Voice Of Old Man's Wife
script.text: Jean, don't stand gossiping, Jean!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (knocking) Jean !

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: (to his wife) Just a moment. Oh dear, dear ... (He closes the door and disappears:)

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: still lying down, his back to the audience, in a hoarse voice

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: What is it?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I've dropped by to see you; Jean.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Who is it?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's me, Berenger. I hope I'm not disturbing you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Oh it's you, is it? Come in!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (trying to open the door) The door's locked.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Just a moment. Oh dear, dear ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN gets up looking pretty terrible. He is wearing green pyjamas, his hair is tousled.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Just a moment.' (He unlocks the door.) Just a moment.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He goes back to bed, gets under the blanket.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Come in!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (coming in) Hello Jean!

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (in bed) What time is it? Aren't you at the office?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're still in bed, you're not at the office, then? Sorry if l'm disturbing you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (still with his back turned) Funny, I didn't recognize your voice.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I didn't recognize yours either.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (still with his back turned) Sitdown!·

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Aren't you feeling well?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN replies with a grunt.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You know Jean, it was stupid of me to get so upset yesterday over a thing like that.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: A thing like what?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yesterday ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: When yesterday? Where yesterday?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Don't you remember? It was about that wretched rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: What rhinoceros?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The rhinoceros, or rather, the two wretched rhinoceroses we saw.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Oh yes, I remember ... How do you know they were wretched?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh I just said that.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Oh. Well let's not talk any more about it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's very nice of you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Then that's that..

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But I would like to say how sorryI am for being so insistent … and so obstinate ... and getting so angry… in fact… I acted stupidly.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: That's not surprising with you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm very sorry.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't feel very well. (He coughs.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's probably why you're in bed. (With a change of tone:) You know, Jean, as it turned out, we were both right.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: What about?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: About… well, you know, the same thing. Sorry to bring it up again, but I'll only mention it briefly. I just wanted you to know that in our different ways we were both right. It's been proved now.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There are some rhinoceroses in the town with two horns and some with one.·

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: That's what I told you! Well, that's just too bad.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, too bad.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Or maybe it's all for the best. It depends. (turning and sitting on his unmade bed, facing

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER) I don't feel well, I don't feel well at all!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh I am sorry! What do you think it is?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't know exactly, there's something wrong somewhere ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you feel weak?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Not at all. On the contrary, I feel full of energy.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps you're too healthy then. Too much energy can be a bad thing. It unsettles·the nervous system.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: My nervous system is in perfect order. (His voice has become more and more hoarse.) I'm sound in mind and limb.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps you've just caught a chill. Have you got a temperature?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't know. Yes, probably I have a touch of fever. My head aches.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Your voice is hoarse, too.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Hoarse?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: A bit hoarse, yes. That's why I didn't recognize it.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Why should I be hoarse? My voice hasn't changed; it's yours that's changed!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Mine?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Why not?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's possible. I hadn't noticed.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I sometimes wonder if you're capable of noticing anything. (Putting his hand to his forehead.) Actually it's my forehead that hurts. I must have hit something. (His voice is even hoarser.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: When did you do that?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't know. I don't remember it happening.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But it must have hurt you. ·

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I must have done it while I was asleep.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The shock would have woken you up. You must have just dreamed you hit something.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I never dream ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Then you've forgotten you dreamed, or rather you only remember subconsciously.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Subconsciously, me? I'm master of my own thoughts, my mind doesn't wander. I think straight, I always think straight.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: If you'd really knocked yourself, you'd have a bump. (Looking at JEAN.) Oh, you've got one, you do have a bump, in fact.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: A bump?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Just a tiny one.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Where?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pointing to JEAN's forehead) There, it starts just above your nose. Have you got a mirror?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (Touching his forehead.) I can feel some-thing. I'm going to have a look in the bathroom.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He gets up abruptly and goes to the bathroom. BERENGER watches him as he goes. Then from the bathroom

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: It's true, I have got a bump. (He comes back; his skin has become greener.) So you see I did knock myself.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You don't look well, your skin is quite–green.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: You seem to delight in saying disagreeable things to me. Have you taken a look at yourself lately?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Forgive me. I didn't mean to upset you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (very hoarse) That's hard to believe.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Your breathing's very heavy. Does your throat hurt? (JEAN goes and sits on his bed again.) If your throat hurts, perhaps it's a touch of tonsillitis.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Why should I have a touch of tonsillitis?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's nothing to be ashamed of– I sometimes get it. Let me feel your pulse. (He rises and takes JEAN'S pulse.)

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (in an even hoarser voice) Oh, it'll pass.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Your pulse is normal. You needn't get alarmed.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I'm not alarmed in the slightest-why should I be?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're right. A few days' rest will put you right.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I've no time to rest. I must go and buy some food.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's not much the matter with you, if you're hungry. But even so, you ought to take a few days' rest. It's wise to take care. Has the doctor been to see you?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't need a doctor.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh but you ought to get the doctor.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't want the doctor. I can look after myself.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You shouldn't reject medical advice.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Doctors invent illnesses that don't exist.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps they do-but after they invent them they cure them.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: who has released JEAN'S wrist, now takes it up again

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Your veins look swollen. They're jutting out.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He examines JEAN's forearm more closely, until JEAN violently withdraws it.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: What do you think you're doing-scrutinizing me as if I were some strange animal?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's your skin... .

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: What's my skin got to do with you? I don't go on about your skin, do I?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's just that it seems to be changing colour all the time. It's going green. (He tries to take JEANS hand.) It's hardening as well.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (withdrawing his hand again) What's the matter with you? You're getting on my nerves.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to himself) Perhaps it's more serious than I thought. (To JEAN:) We must get the doctor. (He goes to the telephone.)

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Leave that thing alone.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He darts over to BERENGER and pushes him. BERENGER staggers.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: You mind your own business.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: All right. It was for your own good.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (coughing and breathing noisily) I know better than you what's good for me.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're breathing very hard.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: One breathes as best one can. You don't like the way I breathe, and I don't like the way you breathe. Your breathing's too feeble, you can't. even hear it; it's as if you were going to drop dead any moment.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Don't get angry with me. You know very well I'm your friend.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: There's no such thing as friendship. I don't believe in your friendship.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's a very hurtful thing to say.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: There's nothing for you to get hurt about.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: My dear Jean ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I'm not your dear Jean.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're probably still angry with me over our silly quarrel yesterday. I admit it was my fault. That's why I came to say I was sorry ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN has been pacing the room like a wild beast in a cage from one wall to the other. BERENGER watches him, occasionally stepping aside to avoid him. JEAN'S voice has become more and more hoarse.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You mustn't excite yourself, it's bad for you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I felt uncomfortable in my clothes; now my pajamas irritate me as well.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He undoes his pajama jacket and does it up again.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But whatever's the matter with your skin?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Can't you leave my skin alone? I certainly wouldn't want to change it for yours.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's gone like leather.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: That makes it more solid. It's weatherproof

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're getting greener and greener.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: You've got color mania today. You're seeing things, you've been drinking again.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I did yesterday, but not today. I promised you to tum over a new leaf. I take notice when friends like you. give me advice. And I never feel humiliated– on the contrary !

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I don't care what you feel. Brrr …

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What did you say?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I didn't say anything. I just went Brrrr ... because I like it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (looking fixedly at JEAN) Do you know what's happened to Boeuf? He's turned into a rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: What happened to Boeuf?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He's turned into a rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (fanning himself with the flaps of his jacket) Brrr ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Come on no, stop joking.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I can puff if I want to can't I? I've every right ... I’m in my own house.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I didn't say you couldn't.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: AndI shouldn't if I were you. I feel hot, I feel hot. Brrr.. Just a moment. I must cool myself down.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (whilst JEAN darts to the bathroom) He must have a fever.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN is in the bathroom, one hears him puffing, and also the sound of running faucet.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (off) Brrr ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He’s' got the shivers. I'm jolly well going to 'phone the doctor.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He goes to the.telephone again then comes back quickly when he hears JEAN's voice.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (off) So old Boeuf turned into a rhinoceros, did he? Ah, ah, ah ! He was just having you on, he'd disguised himself

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He pokes his head round the bathroom door, He is very green.' The bump over his nose is slightly larger.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: He was just disguised.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (walking about the room, without seeing JEAN) He looked very serious about it, I assure you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Oh well, that's his business.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: turning to JEAN who disappears again into the bathroom

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm sure he didn't do it on purpose. He didn't want to change.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (off) How do you know?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: · Well, everything led one to suppose so.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: And what if he did do it on purpose? Eh? What if he did it on purpose?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'd be very surprised. At any rate, Mrs. Boeuf didn't seem to know about it …

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (in a very hoarse voice) Ah, ah, ah! Old Mrs. Boeuf She's just a fool!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well fool or no fool ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: he enters swiftly, takes off his jacket, and throws it on the bed. BERENGER discreetly averts his gaze. JEAN, whose back and chest are now green, goes back into the bathroom.As he walks in and out;

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Boeuf never let his wife know what he was up to ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're wrong there, Jean-it was a very united family.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Very united, was it? Are you sure? Hum, hum, Brr ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: moving to the bathroom, where JEAN slams the door in his face

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Very united. And the proof is that ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (from within) Boeuf led his own private life. He had a secret side to him deep down which he kept to himself.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I shouldn't make you talk, it seems to upset you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: On the contrary, it relaxes me.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Even so, let me call the doctor, I beg you.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I absolutely forbid it'. I can't stand obstinate people.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN comes back into the bedroom. BERENGER backs away a little scared, for JEAN is greener than ever and speaks only with difficulty. His voice is unrecognizable.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Well, whether he changes into a rhinoceros on purpose or against his will, he's probably all the better for it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How can you say a thing like that? Surely you don't think ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: You always see the black side of everything. It obviously gave him great pleasure to turn into a rhinoceros. There's nothing extraordinary in that.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's nothing extraordinary in it, but I doubt if it gave him much pleasure.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: And why not?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's hard to say exactly why; it's just something you feel.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: I tell you it's not as bad as all that. After all, rhinoceroses are living creatures the same as us; they've got as much right to life as we have!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: As long as they don't destroy ours in the process. You must admit the difference in.mentality.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: pacing up and down the room, and in and out of the bathroom

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Are you under the impression that our way of life is superior?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well at any rate, we have our own moral standards which I consider incompatible with the standards of these animals.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Moral standards! I'm sick of moral standards! We need to go beyond moral standards ! .

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What would you put in their place?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (still pacing) Nature!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Nature?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Nature has its own laws. Morality is against Nature.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Are you suggesting we replace our moral laws by the law of the jungle?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: It would suit me, suit me fine.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You say that. But deep down, no one ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (interrupting him, pacing up and down) We've got to build our life on new foundations. We must get back to primeval integrity:

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't agree with you at all.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (breathing noisily) I can't-breathe.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Just think for a moment. You must admit that we have a philosophy that animals don't share, and an irreplaceable set of values, which it's taken centuries of human civilization to build up...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (in the bathroom) When we've demolished all that, we'll be better off! ·

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I know you don't mean that seriously. You're joking! It's just a poetic fancy.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Brrr. (He almost trumpets.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'd never realized you were a poet.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (comes out of the bathroom) Brrr. (He trumpets again.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's not what you believe fundamentally-I know you too well. You know as well as I do that mankind ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (interrupting him) Don't talk to me about mankind!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I mean the human individual, humanism ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Humanism is all washed up! You're a ridiculous old sentimentalist. (He goes into the bathroom.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But you must admit that the mind ...

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (from the bathroom) Just cliches ! You're talking rubbish!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Rubbish!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: from the bathroom in a very hoarse voice, difficult to understand

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Utter rubbish!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm amazed to hear you say that, Jean, really! You must be out of your mind. You wouldn't like to be a rhinoceros yourself, now would you?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Why not? I'm not a victim of prejudice like you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Can you speak more clearly? I didn't catch what you said. You swallowed the words.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (still in the bathroom) Then keep your ears open.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What?

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: Keep your ears open. I said what's wrong with being a rhinoceros? I'm all for change

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's not like you to say a thing like that ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER stops short for JEAN's appearance is truly alarming. JEAN has become, in fact, completely green: The bump on his forehead is practically a rhinoceros horn.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh! You really must be out of your mind!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: JEAN dashes to his bed, throws the covers on the floor, talking in a fast and furious gabble16, and making very weird sounds.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You. mustn't get into such a state-calm down! I hardly recognize you any more.

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (hardly distinguishable) Hot. Far too hot! Demolish the lot, clothes itch, they itch! (He drops his pajama trousers.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What are you doing? You're not yourself! You're generally so modest !

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He lunges towards BERENGER, head down. BERENGER gets out of the way.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Watch out!

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (puffing noisily) Sorry! (He darts at great speed into the bathroom) .

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: makes as if to escape by the door left, then comes back and goes into the bathroom after JEAN, saying

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I really can't leave him like that-after all he is a friend. (From the bathroom) I'm going to get the doctor! It's absolutely necessary, believe me!

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (from the bathroom) No!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (from the bathroom) Calm down, Jean, you're being ridiculous! Oh, your horn's getting longer and longer-you're a rhinoceros ! ·

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (from the bathroom) I'll trample you, I'll trample you down!

script.speaker: Jean
script.text: (Alot·of noise comes from the bathroom trumpetings, objects falling, the sound of a shattered mirror; then BERENGER reappears, very frightened; he closes the bathroom door with difficulty against the resistance that is being made from inside.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pushing against the door) He's a….rhinoceros, he's a rhinoceros !

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER manages to close the door. As he does so, his coat is pierced by a rhinoceros horn. The door shakes under the animal's constant pressure and the din continues in the bathroom; trumpetings are heard_, interspersed with indistinct phrases such as: 'I'm furious! The swine!' etc. BERENGER rushes to the door right.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I never would have thought it of him-never! He opens the staircase door and goes and knocks at the landing door; he bangs repeatedly on it with his fist.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's a rhinoceros in the building ! Get the police!

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: (poking his head out) What's the matter?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Get the police·! There's a rhinoceros in the house!

script.speaker: Voice Of Old Man's Wife
script.text: What are you up to, Jean? Why are you making all that noise?

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: (to his wife) I don't know what he's talking about. He's seen a rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, here in the house. Get the police!

script.speaker: Old Man
script.text: What do you think you're up to, disturbing people like that. What a way to behave! (He shuts the door in his face.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (rushing to the stairs) Porter, porter, there's a rhinoceros in the house, get the police ! Porter !

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The upper part of the porter's lodge is seen to open; the head of a rhinoceros appears.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Another!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER rushes upstairs again. He wants to go back into. JEAN's room, hesitates, then makes for the door of the OLD MAN again. At this moment the door of the room opens to reveal two rhinoceros heads.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh, my God!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER goes back into JEAN's room where the bathroom door is still shaking. He goes to the window which is represented simply by the frame, facing the audience. He is exhausted, almost fainting; he murmurs.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: My God! Oh my God! He makes a gigantic effort, and manages to get astride the window (that is, towards the audience) but gets back again quickly. For at the same time, crossing the orchestra pit at great speed, move a large number of rhinoceros heads in line.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: BERENGER gets back with all speed, looks out of the window for a moment.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's a whole herd of them in the street now! An army of rhinoceroses, surging up the avenue! (He looks all around) Where can I get out? Where can I get out? If only they'd keep to the middle of the road! They're all over the pavement as well.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Where can I get out? Distracted, he goes from door to door and to the window, whilst the bathroom door continues to shake and JEAN continues to trumpet and hurl incomprehensible insults.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: This continues for some moments; whenever BERENGER in his disordered attempts to escape reaches the doorway, he is greeted by rhinoceros heads which trumpet and cause him to beat a hasty retreat. He goes to the window for the last time and looks out.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: A whole herd of them! And they always said the rhinoceros was a solitary animal ! (He wrings his hands.) What's to be done? He goes once more to the various exits, but the spectacle of the rhinoceros halts him.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: When he gets back to the bathroom door it seems about to give way. BERENGER throws himself against the back wall, which falls; the street is visible in the background; he flees, shouting

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Rhinoceros ! Rhinoceros ! Noises. The bathroom door is on the point of yielding

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: END OF ACT TWO.
ACT THREE
SCENE ONE: CHEZ BERENGER

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The arrangement is roughly the same as in the previous scene. It is BERENGER's room, which bears a striking resemblance to that of JEAN. Only certain details, one or- two extra pieces of furniture, reveal that it is a different room. Staircase to the left, and landing. Door at the end of the landing. There is no porter's lodge. Up-stage is a divan. An armchair, and a little table with a telephone. Perhaps an extra telephone, and a chair. Window up-stage, open. A window frame in the foreground…BERENGER is lying on his divan, his back to the audience. BERENGER is lying fully dressed. His head is bandaged. He seems to be having a bad dream, and writhes in his sleep.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No. (Pause) Watch out for the horns! (Pause) The noise of a considerable number of rhinoceroses is heard passing under the upstage window.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No! He falls to the floor still fighting with what he has seen in his dream, and wakes up. He puts his hand to his head with an apprehensive air, then moves to the mirror and lifts his bandage, as the noises fade away.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He heaves a sigh of relief when he sees he has no bump. He hesitates, goes to the divan, lies down, and instantly gets up again. He goes to the table where he takes up a bottle of brandy and a glass, and is about to pour himself a drink.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Then after a short internal struggle he replaces the bottle and glass.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Come on, where's your will-power! He wants to go back to his divan, but the rhinoceroses are heard again under the up-stage window. The noises stop; he goes to the little table, hesitates a moment, then with a gesture of ‘Oh what's· it matter!'

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: he pours himself a glass of brandy. which he downs at one go. He puts the bottle and glass back in place. He coughs. His cough seems to worry him; he coughs again and listens hard to the sound.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He looks at himself again in the mirror, coughing, then opens the window; the panting of the animals becomes louder; he coughs again.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No, it's not the same·! He calms down, shuts the window, feels his bandaged forehead, goes to his divan, and seems to fall asleep.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DUDARD is seen mounting the top stairs; he gets to the landing and knocks on BERENGER's door.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (starting up) What is it?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I've dropped by to see you, Berenger.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Who is it? ,

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's me.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Who's me?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Me, Dudard.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Ah, it's you, come in!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I hope I'm not disturbing you. (He tries to open the door.) The door's locked.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Just a moment. Oh dear, dear! (He opens the door. DUDARD enters.)

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Hello Berenger.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Hello Dudard, what time is it?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: So, you're still barricaded in your room! Feeling any better, old man?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Forgive me, I didn't recognize your voice. (Goes to open the window.) Yes, yes, I think I'm a bit better.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: My voice hasn't changed. I recognized yours easily enough.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm sorry, I thought that ... you're right, your voice is quite normal. Mine hasn't changed either, has it?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Why should it have changed?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm not a bit ... a bit hoarse, am I?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Not that I notice.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's good. That's very reassuring.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Why, what's the matter with you?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't know–does one ever know? Voices can suddenly change !

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Have you caught a cold, as well?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I hope not…I sincerely hope not. But do sit down, Dudard, take a seat. Sit in the armchair.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (sitting in the armchair) Are you still feeling a bit off colour? Is your head still bad? (He points to BERENGER' s bandage.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh yes, I've still got a headache. But there's no bump, I haven't knocked. myself ... have I?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He lifts the bandage, shows his forehead to DUDARD

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, there's no bump as far as I can see.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I hope there never will be. Never.·

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What's the matter with you? You're all nervous and agitated. It must be your migraine. You just stay quiet and you'll feel better.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Migraine ! Don't talk to me about migraines! Don't talk about them !

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's understandable that you've got a migraine after all that emotion.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (darting to the mirror, lifting the bandage) Nothing there ... You know, it can all start from something like that.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What can all start?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm frightened of becoming someone. else.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Calm yourself; now, and sit down. Dashing up and down the room like that can only make you more nervous.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're right, I must keep calm. (He goes and sits down.) I just can't get over it, you know.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: About Jean you mean? –I know.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, Jean, of course– and the others, too.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I realize it must have been a shock to you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Jean was my best friend. Then to watch him change before my eyes, and the way he got so furious ! .

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I know. You felt let down; I understand. Try and not think about it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How can I help thinking about it? He was such a warm-hearted person, always.so human! Who'd have thought it of him ! We'd known each other for years. He was the last person I'd have expected to change like that. I felt more sure of him than of myself!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And then to do that to me!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I'm sure he didn't do it specially to annoy you!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It seemed as if he did. If you'd seen the state he was in ... the expression on his face…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's just that you happened to be with him at the time. It would have been the same no matter who was there.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But after all our years together he might have controlled himself in front of me.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You think everything revolves round you, you think that everything that happens concerns you personally; you're not the centre of the universe, you know.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps you're right. I must try to readjust myself, but the phenomenon in itself is so disturbing. To tell the truth, it absolutely shatters me. What can be the explanation?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: For the moment I haven't found a satisfactory explanation. I observe the facts, and I take them in. They exist, so they must have an explanation.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I understand what you mean, at least I'm trying to.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: So why get upset over a few cases of rhinoceritis. Perhaps it's just another disease.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Exactly! And I'm frightened of catching it.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Oh stop thinking about it. Really, you attach too much importance to the whole business. In my opinion– if you'll excuse me saying this about your friend– he was.far too excitable, a bit wild, and eccentric.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You shouldn’t base your opinions on exceptional cases. It's the average case you must consider.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, of course, he must have been in a critical condition to have got himself into that state. He must have been temporarily unbalanced. And yet he gave his reasons for it, he'd obviously given it a lot of thought, and weighed the pros and cons ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And what about Boeuf then, was he unbalanced, too ...  and what about all the others ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: There's still the epidemic theory. It's like influenza. It's not the first time there's been an epidemic.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's never been one like this.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: In any case you can be sure that Boeuf and the others didn't do what they did–become what they became–just-to annoy you. They wouldn't have gone to that trouble.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's true, that makes sense, it's a reassuring thought... or on the other hand, perhaps that makes it worse? Rhinoceroses are heard, galloping under the up-stage window.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There, you hear that? (He darts to the window.)

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Oh, why can't you leave them alone!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER closes the window again.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: They're not doing you any harm. Really, you're obsessed by them ! It's not good for you. You're wearing yourself out. You've had one shock, why look for more? You just concentrate on getting back to normal.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I wonder if I really am immune?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: In any case it's not fatal. Certain illnesses are good for you. I'm convinced this is something you can cure if you want to. They'll get over it, you'll see.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But it's bound to ·have certain after-effects! An organic upheaval like that can't help but leave….

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's only temporary, don't you worry.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Are you absolutely certain?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I think so, yes, I suppose so.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you feel like a brandy?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He goes to the table where the bottle stands.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Not for me, thank you, I never touch it. But don't mind me if you want some-you go ahead, don't worry about me. But watch out, it may make your headache worse.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Alcohol is good for epidemics. It immunizes you. It kills influenza microbes, for instance.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Perhaps it doesn't kill all microbes. They don't know about rhinoceritis yet.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Jean never touched alcohol. He just pretended to. Maybe that's -why he ... perhaps that explains his attitude. (He offers a full glass to DUDARD) You're sure you won't?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, no, never·before lunch, thank you.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER empties his glass, continues to hold it together with the bottle in his hands. He coughs.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You see, you can't take it. It makes you cough.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (worried) Yes, it did make me cough. How did I cough?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Like everyone coughs when they drink something a bit strong.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: moving to put the glass and bottle back on the table

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There wasn't anything odd about it, was there? It was a real human cough? '

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What are you getting at? It was an ordinary human cough. What other sort of cough could it have been?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't know ... Perhaps an animal's cough. Do rhinoceroses cough?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Look; Berenger, you're being ridiculous, you invent difficulties for yourself, you ask yourself the weirdest questions ... I remember you said yourself that the best protection against the thing was willpower.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, I did.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well then, prove you've got some.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I have, I assure you ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Prove it to yourself– don't drink any more brandy. You'll feel more sure of yourself then.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You deliberately misunderstand me. I told you the only reason I take it is because it keeps the worst at bay; I'm doing it quite deliberately. When the epidemic's over, then I shall stop drinking. I'd already decided that before the whole business began.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I must put it off for the time being!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You're inventing excuses for yourself.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you think I am? In any case, that's got nothing to do with what's happening now.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: How do we know?

script.speaker: Berenger
