script.text: (alarmed) Do you really think so? You think that's how the rot sets in? I'm not an alcoholic. (He goes to the mirror and examines himself.) Do you think, by any chance… (He touches his face, pats his bandaged forehead.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Nothing's changed; it hasn't done any harm so it must have done good or it's harmless at any rate.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I was only joking. I was just teasing· you. You see the black side of everything–watch out, or you'll become neurotic. When you've got over your shock completely and you can get out for.a breath of fresh air, you'll feel better–you'll see!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Go out? I suppose I'll have to. I'm dreading the moment. I'll be bound to meet some of them ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What if you do? You only have to keep out of their way. And there aren't as many as all that.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I see them all over the place. You'll probably say that's being morbid, too.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: They don't attack you. If you leave them alone, they just ignore you. You can't say they're spiteful. They've even got a certain natural innocence, a sort of frankness. Besides I walked right along the avenue to get to you today.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I got here safe and sound, didn't I? No trouble at all.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Just the sight of them upsets me. It's a nervous thing. I don't get angry-no, it doesn't pay to get angry, you never know where it'll lead to, I watch out for that..But it does something to me, here! (He points to his heart.) I get a tight feeling inside.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I think you're right to a certain extent to have some reaction. But you go too far. You've no sense of humour, that's your trouble, none at all. You must learn to be more detached, and try and see the funny side of things.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I feel responsible for everything that happens. I feel involved, I just can't be indifferent.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Judge not lest ye be judged. If you start worrying about everything that happens you'd never be able to go on living.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: If only it had happened somewhere else, in some other country, and we'd just read about it in the papers, we could discuss it quietly, examine the question from all points of view and come to an objective conclusion.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But when you're involved yourself, when you suddenly find yourself up against the brutal facts –the shock is too violent for you to stay cool and detached. I'm frankly surprised, I'm very very surprised. I can't get over it.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well I'm surprised, too. Or rather I was. Now I'm starting to get used to it. ·

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Your nervous system is better balanced than mine. You're lucky. But don't you agree it's all very unfortunate ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (interrupting him) I don't say it's a good thing. And don't get the idea that I'm on the rhinoceroses' side ... More sounds .of rhinoceroses passing, this time under the down-stage window-frame.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (with a start) There they are, there they are again! Oh, it's no use, I just can't get used to them. I can't sleep at night. I get insomnia. I doze off during the day out of sheer exhaustion.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Take some sleeping tablets.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's not the answer. If I sleep, it's worse. I dream about them, I get nightmares.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That's what comes of taking things too seriously. Admit it, you get a kick out of torturing yourself.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm not a masochist, I assure you.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Then face the facts and get over it. This is the situation and there's nothing you can do about it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's fatalism.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's common sense. When a thing like this happens there's bound to be a reason for it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (getting up) Well, I don't want to accept the situation.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What else can you do? What are your plans?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't know for the moment. I must think it over. I will write to the papers; I'll draw up manifestos; I will apply for an audience with the mayor–or his deputy, if the mayor's too busy.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You leave the authorities to do what they think best! I still think it's not all that serious. I think it’s silly to get worked up just because a few people decide to change into rhinoceroses..

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There you are, you see! If our leaders and fellow citizens all think like you, they'll never take any action.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You wouldn't want to ask for help from abroad, surely? This is an internal affair; it only concerns our country.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I believe in international solidarity ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You're a Don Quixote. Oh, I don't mean that nastily, don't be offended! I'm only saying it for your own good, because you really need to calm down.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're right, I know–forgive me. I get too worked up. But I'll change, I will change. I'm sorry to keep you all this time listening to my ramblings. You must have work to do. Did you get my application for sick leave?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Don't worry about that. It's all in order. In any case, the office hasn't resumed work.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Haven't they repaired the staircase yet? What negligence!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: They're repairing it now. But it's slow work. It's not easy to find the workmen. They sign on and work for a couple of days, then don't turn up any more. You never see them again. Then you have to look for others.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And they talk about unemployment! At least I hope we're getting a stone staircase.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, it's wood again, but new wood this time.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh! The way these organizations stick to the old routine. They throw money down the drain but when it's needed for something really useful they pretend they can't afford it. I bet Mr. Papillon's none too pleased. He was dead set on having a stone staircase.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What's he say about it?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: We haven't got a Chief any more. Mr. Papillon's resigned.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's not possible!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's true, I assure you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well, I’m amazed. .,. Was it on account of the staircase?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: He's retiring to the country.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Retiring? He's not the age. He might still have become the Director.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: He's given it all up! Said he needed a rest.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I bet the management's pretty upset to see him go; they'll have to replace him. All your diplomas should come in useful–you stand a good chance.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I suppose I might as well tell you–it's really rather funny–the fact is, he turned into a rhinoceros. Distant rhinoceros noises.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: A rhinoceros!!!! Mr.Papillon a rhinoceros! I can't believe it ! I don't think it's funny at all! Why didn't you tell me before?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well you know you have no sense of humour. I didn't want to tell you because I knew very well you wouldn't see the funny side, and it would upset you. You know how impressionable you are!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (raising his arms to heaven) Oh that's awful Mr. Papillon ! And he had such a good job.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That proves his metamorphosis was sincere.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He couldn't have done it on purpose. I'm certain it must have been involuntary.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: How can we tell? It's hard to know the real reasons for people's decisions.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He must have made a mistake. He let himself be talked into it, I feel sure.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It could happen to anybody !

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (alarmed) To·anybody? Oh no, not to you it couldn't–could it? And not to me!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: We must hope not.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Because we don't want to ... that's so, isn't it? Tell me, that is so, isn't it?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Yes, yes, of course ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (a little calmer) I still would have thought Mr. Papillon would have had the strength to resist. I thought he had a bit more character! What possible material or moral interest could he have had?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It was obviously a disinterested gesture on his part.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Obviously. There were extenuating circumstances ...or were they aggravating? Aggravating, I should think, because if he did it by choice ... You know, I feel sure that Botard must have taken a very poor view of it–what did he think of his Chief's behaviour?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Oh poor old Botard was quite indignant, absolutely outraged. I've rarely seen anyone so incensed.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well for once I'm on his side. He's a good man after all. A man of sound common sense. And to think I misjudged him.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: He misjudged you, too.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That proves how objective I'm being now. Besides, you had a pretty bad opinion of him yourself

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I wouldn't say I had a bad opinion. I admit I didn't often agree with him. I never liked his scepticism, the way he was always so suspicious. There was nothing precise or objective about the way Botard argued.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I don't approve of the rhinoceroses myself, as you know–not at all, don't go thinking that! But Botard's attitude was too passionate, as usual, and therefore over-simplified. His opinion seems to me like it is entirely determined by hatred of his superiors.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What’s more –he talks in cliches.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well forgive me, but this time I'm in complete agreement with Botard. I shall congratulate him when I see him. I deplore Mr. Papillon's action, it was his duty not to give in.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: How intolerant you are! Maybe Papillon felt the need for a bit of relaxation after all these years of office life.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (ironically) And you're too tolerant. far too broad-minded!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: My dear Berenger, one must always make an effort to understand. We must try to do this because, after all, we are thinking beings. One has to keep an open mind– that's essential to a scientific mentality. Everything is logical. To understand is to justify.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You'll be siding with the rhinoceroses before long.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, no, not at all. I wouldn't go that far. I'm simply trying to look the facts unemotionally in the face. I'm trying to be realistic. I also contend that there is no real evil in what occurs naturally. I don't believe in seeing evil in everything.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And you consider all this natural?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: –what could be more natural than a rhinoceros?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, but for a man to turn into a rhinoceros is abnormal beyond question.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well, of course, that's a matter of opinion ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It is beyond question, absolutely beyond question!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You seem very sure of yourself. Who can say where the normal stops and the abnormal begins? Nobody has solved this problem yet, either medically or philosophically·. You ought to know that. .

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The problem may not be resolved philosophically-but in practice it's simple. They may “prove” there's no such thing as movement ... and then you start walking ... (He starts walking up and down the room.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: and you go on walking, and you say to yourself, like Galileo, 'and yet it moves'...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You're getting things all mixed up! Don't confuse the issue. In Galileo's case it was the opposite: theoretic and scientific thought proving itself superior to mass opinion and dogmatism.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (quite lost) What does all that mean? You don't know what's normal and what isn't normal any more. I couldn't care less about Galileo ... I don't give a damn about Galileo!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You brought him up in the first place! You said that practical application always has the last word. Maybe it does, but only when it proceeds from theory! The history of thought and science proves that!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (more and more furious) It doesn't prove anything of the sort! It's all gibberish, utter lunacy!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: There again we need to define exactly what we mean by lunacy ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Lunacy is lunacy and that's all there is to it! Everybody knows what lunacy is.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You're getting all heated up. Our opinions may not exactly coincide but we can still discuss the matter peaceably. These things should be discussed.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (distracted) You think I'm getting all heated up, do you? I might be…like Jean. Oh no, no, I don't want to become like him. I mustn't be like him. (He calms down.) I'm not very well versed in philosophy. I've never studied; you've got all sorts of diplomas.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's why you're so·at ease in discussion, whereas I never know what to answer– I'm so clumsy.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: Louder rhinoceros noises passing. First tinder the up-stage window and then the down-stage.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But I do feel you're in the wrong… feel it instinctively–no, that's not what I mean, it's the rhinoceros' which has instinct-I feel it intuitively, yes, that's the word, intuitively.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What do you mean by 'intuitive'?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Intuitively means ... I feel it, just like that. I think your excessive tolerance, and your generous indulgence ... believe me, they're really only weakness… just blind spots…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You're innocent enough to think that.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You'll always be able to dance rings round me. But, you know what? I'm going to try and get hold of the Logician…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: What logician?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The Logician, the philosopher, a logician, you know. . .you know better than I do what a logician is. A logician I met, who explained to me…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: – What did he explain to you?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He explained that the Asian rhinoceroses were African and the African ones Asian .

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I don't follow you.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No…no ... he proved the contrary—that the African ones were Asian and the Asian ones ... I know what I mean. That's not what I wanted to say. But you'll get along very well with him. He's your sort of person, a very good man, a very subtle mind, brilliant.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Increasing noises from the rhinoceroses. The words of the two men are drowned by the animals passing under the windows; for a few moments the lips of DUDARD and

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER are seen to move without any words being heard.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There they go again! Will they never stop! (He runs to the up-stage window.) Stop it! Stop it! You devils!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The rhinoceroses move away. BERENGER shakes his fist after them.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (seated) I'd be happy to meet your Logician. If he can enlighten me on these obscure and delicate points, I'd be only too delighted.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (as he runs to the down-stage window) Yes, I'll bring him along, he'll talk to you. He's a very distinguished person, you'll see. (To the rhinoceroses,from the window.) You devils! (Shakes his fist as before.) •

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Let them alone. And be more polite. You shouldn't talk to people like that ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (still at the window) There they go again! A boater hat pierced by a rhinoceros horn emerges from the orchestra pit under the window and passes swiftly from left to right.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's a hat impaled on a rhinoceros horn. Oh, it's the Logician's hat! It's the Logician's! That's the damned limit! The Logician's turned into a rhinoceros!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That's no reason to be coarse!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Dear Lord, who can you turn to-who? I ask you! The Logician– a rhinoceros !

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (going to the window) Where is he?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pointing) There, that one there, you see!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: He's the only rhinoceros in a boater hat! That makes you think. You're sure it's your Logician?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The Logician ... a rhinoceros!!!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: He's still retained a vestige of his old individuality.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: shakes his fist again at the straw-hatted rhinoceros, which has disappeared

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'll never join up with you! Not me!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: If he was a genuine thinker, as you say, he must have weighed all the pros and and cons before deciding.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: still shouting after the ex-Logician and the other rhinoceroses who have moved away

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'll never join up with you!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (settling into the armchair) Yes, it certainly makes you think.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER closes the down-stage window; goes to the up-stage window where other rhinoceroses are passing, presumably making a tour of the house. He opens the window and shouts.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No, I'll never join up with you!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (aside, in his armchair) They're going round and round the house. They're playing! Just big babies!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY has been seen mounting the top. stairs. She knocks on BERENGER's door. She is carrying a basket.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: There's somebody at the door, Berenger!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He takes BERENGER, who is still at the window, by the sleeve.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (shouting after the rhinoceroses) It's a disgrace, masquerading like this, a disgrace!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: There's someone knocking, Berenger, can't you hear?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Open, then, if you want to!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He continues to watch the rhinoceroses whose noise is fading away. DUDARD goes to open the door.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (coming in) Morning, Mr. Dudard.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Oh, it's you, Miss Daisy.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Is Berenger here, is he any better?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: How nice to see you, my dear. Do you often visit Berenger?.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Where is he?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (pointing) There.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: He's all on his own, poor thing. And he's not very well at the moment, somebody has to give him a hand.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You're a good friend, Miss Daisy.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: That's just what I am, a good friend.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You've got a warm heart.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'm a good friend, that's all.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (turning, leaving the window open) Oh Miss Daisy! How kind of you to come, how very kind!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It certainly is.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Did you know, Miss Daisy, that the Logician is a rhinoceros?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, I did. I caught sight of him in the street as I arrived. He was running very fast for someone his age! Are you feeling any better, Mr. .Berenger?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: My head's still bad! Still got a headache! Isn't it frightful? What do you think about it?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I think you ought to be resting ... you should take things quietly for a few more days.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BERENGER and DAISY) I hope I'm not disturbing

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DAISY) I meant about the Logician ...

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to DUDARD) Why should you be? (To BERENGER:) Oh, about the Logician? I don't think anything at all!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to DAISY) I thought I might be in the way!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BERENGER) What do you expect me to think? (To both:) I've got some news for you: Botard's a rhinoceros!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well, well !

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't believe it. He was against it. You must be mistaken. He protested. Dudard has just been telling me. Isn't that so, Dudard? .

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That is so.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I know he was against it. But it didn't stop him turning, twenty-four hours after Mr. Papillon.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well, he must have changed his mind! Everybody has the right to do that.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Then obviously anything can happen!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BERENGER) He was a very good man according to you just now.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to. DAISY) I just can't believe you. They must have lied to you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I saw him do it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Then he must have been lying, he was just pretending.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: He seemed very sincere.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Did he give any reasons?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: What he said was: we must move with the times! Those were his last human words.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Move with the times! What a mentality! What childishness! (He makes a wide gesture.) But now that I think about it, Botard's behaviour doesn't surprise me.. Good men make good rhinoceroses, unfortunately. It's because they are so good that they get taken in.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Do you mind if I put this basket on the table? (She does so.) .

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But he was a good man with a lot of resentment ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to DAISY, and hastening to help her with the basket) Excuse me, excuse us both, we should have given you a hand before.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (continues) ... He was riddled with hatred for his superiors, and he'd got an inferiority complex ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (to BERENGER) Your argument doesn't hold water, because the example he followed was the Chief's, making him the instrument of the very people who ‘exploited’ him, as he used to say.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: No, it seems to me that with him it was a case of community spirit triumphing over his impulses toward anarchy.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's the rhinoceroses who practice anarchy, because they're in the minority.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: They are, it's true– for now.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They're a pretty big minority, and getting bigger all the time. My cousin's a rhinoceros now, and his wife. Not to mention public figures like the Arch Bishop.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: A church leader!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: And the cardinal.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: This is going to spread to other countries, you'll see.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And to think it all started with us!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: ..and some of the aristocracy. And others, too. Lots of others. Maybe a quarter of the whole town.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: We're still in the majority. We must take advantage of that. We must do something before we're overwhelmed.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Well for the moment, let's eat. I've brought some food.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're very kind, Miss Daisy.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (aside) Very kind indeed.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't know how to thank you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to DUDARD) Would you care to stay with us?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I don't want to be a nuisance.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Whatever do you mean, Mr. Dudard? You know very well we’d love you to stay.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Well, you know, I'd hate to be in the way ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Of course, stay, Dudard. It's always a pleasure to talk

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: As a matter of fact I'm in a bit of a hurry.I have an appointment.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Just now you said·you had nothing to do.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (unpacking her basket) You know, I had a lot of trouble finding food. The shops have been plundered; they just devour everything. And a lot of the shops are closed. It's written up outside: 'Closed on account of transformation.'

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They should be all rounded up in a big enclosure, and kept under strict supervision.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That's easier said than done. The animals' protection league would be the first to object.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: And besides everyone has a close relative or a friend among them, and that would make it even more difficult.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: So everybody's mixed up in it!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: Everybody's in the same boat!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But how can people be rhinoceroses? It doesn't bear thinking about! (To DAISY) Shall I help you set the table?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: No, don't bother. I know where the plates are.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She goes to a cupboard and takes out plates.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (aside) She's obviously very familiar with the place ...

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to DUDARD) I'm setting for three–all right? You are staying with us?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DUDARD) Yes, of course you're staying.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BERENGER) You get used to it, you know. Nobody seems surprised any more to see herds of rhinoceroses galloping through the streets. They just stand aside, and then carry on as if nothing had happened.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's the wisest action to take.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well I can't get used.to it.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (reflectively) I wonder if one oughtn't to give it a try?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Well right now, let's have lunch.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't see how a legal man like yourself can ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: A great noise of rhinoceroses travelling very fast is heard outside. Trumpets and drums are also heard.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What's going on? (They rush to the down-stage window.) What is it? The sound of a wall crumbling is heard. Dust covers part of the stage, enveloping , if possible, the characters. They are heard speaking through it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You can't see a thing! What's happening?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: You can't see, but you can hear all right.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That's no good!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: The plates will be all covered in dust.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How unhygienic !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Let's hurry up and eat. We won't pay any attention to them.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The dust disperses.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pointing into the auditorium) They've demolished the walls of the Fire Station.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: That's true, they've demolished them!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: who after moving from the window to near the table holding the plate which she is endeavouring to clean, rushes to join the other two

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They're coming out.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: All the firemen, a whole regiment of rhinoceroses, led by drums.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They're pouring up the streets!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's gone too far, much too far!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: More rhinoceroses are streaming out of the courtyard.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And out of the houses ...

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: And the windows as well !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They're joining up with the others. A man comes out of the landing door left and .dashes downstairs at top speed; then another with a large horn on·his nose; then a woman wearing an entire rhinoceros head.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: There aren't enough of us left any more.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How many with one horn, and how many with two?

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: The statisticians are bound to be compiling statistics now. There’ll be plenty of intellectual controversy you can be sure!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They can only calculate approximately. It's all happening so fast. It leaves them no time. No time to calculate.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: The best thing is to let the statisticians handle it. Come and eat, my dear. That'll calm you down. You'll feel better afterwards. (To DUDARD) And you, too.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: They move away from the window. DAISY takes BERENGER's arm; he allows himself to be led docilely. DUDARD suddenly halts.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I don't feel very hungry-or rather, to be frank, I don't like tinned food very much. I feel like eating outside on the grass.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You mustn't do that. Think of the risk!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: But really I don't want to put you to the trouble.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But we've already told you…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: (interrupting BERENGER) I really mean it.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to DUDARD) Of course if you really don't want to stay, we can't force you…

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I didn't mean to offend you.-

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DAISY) Don't let him go, he mustn't go.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'd like him to stay… but people must do as they please.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DUDARD) Man is superior to the rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I didn't say he wasn't. But I'm not with you absolutely either. I don't know.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (to DUDARD) You're weakening too, Dudard. It's just a passing phase which you'll regret.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: If it's just a passing phase threat!- there's no great danger.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I feel certain scruples! I feel it's my duty to stick by my employers and my friends, through thick and thin.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's not as if you were married to them.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I've renounced marriage. I prefer the great universal family to the little domestic one.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (softly) We shall miss·you a lot, Dudard, but we can't do anything about it.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: It's my duty to stick by them; .I have to do my duty.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No you're wrong, your duty is to…you don't see where your real duty lies ... your duty is to oppose them, with a firm, clear mind!

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: I will keep my mind clear.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He starts to move round the stage in circles.

script.speaker: Dudard
script.text: As clear as ever it was. But if you're going to criticize, it's better to do so from the inside. I'm not going to abandon them. I won't abandon them.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: He's very good-hearted.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He's too good-hearted. (To DUDARD, then dashing to the door) You're too good-hearted, you're human. (To DAISY) Don't let him go. He's making a mistake. He's human.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: What can I do?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DUDARD opens the door and runs off; he goes down the stairs at top speed followed by BERENGER who shouts after him from the landing.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Come back, Dudard ! We' re fond of you, don't go! It's too late! (He comes back.) Too late!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: We couldn't do anything.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She closes the door behind BERENGER, who darts to the window.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He's joined up with them. Where is he now?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (moving to the window) With them.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Which one is he?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You can't tell. You can't recognize him anymore.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They all look alike, all alike. (To DAISY:) He did hesitate. You should have held him back by force.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I didn't dare to.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You should :have been firmer with him, you should have insisted; he was in love with you, wasn't he ?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: He never made me any official declaration. .

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Everybody knew he was. He's done. this out of thwarted love. He was a shy man. He wanted to make a big gesture to impress you. Don't you feel like going after him?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Not at all. Or I wouldn't be here!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (looking out,of the window) You can see nothing but them in the street. (He darts to the up-stage window.) Nothing but them ! You were wrong, Daisy. (He looks through the down-stage window again.) Not a single human being as far as the eye can see.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're all over the street. Half with one horn and half with two, and that's the only distinction ! Powerful noises of moving rhinoceroses are heard, but somehow it is a musical sound.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: On the up-stage wall stylized heads appear and disappear; they become more and more numerous from now on until the end of the play. Towards the end they stay fixed for longer and longer, until eventually they fill the entire back wall, remaining static.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The heads, in spite of their monstrous appearance, seem to become more and more beautiful.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: ·You don't feel let down, do you, Daisy? There's nothing you regret?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: No, no

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: :I want so much to be a comfort to you.I love you, Daisy, don't ever leave me.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Shut the window, darling. They're making such a noise. And. the dust is rising even up to here. Everything will get filthy.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, you're right.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He closes the down-stage window and DAISY closes the up-stage one. They meet centre-stage.} I'm not afraid of anything as long as we're together. I don't care what happens. You know, Daisy, I thought I'd never be able to fall in love again. (He takes her hands, strokes her arms.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Well you see, everything is possible.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I want so much to make you happy. Do you think you can be happy with me.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Why not? If you're happy, then I'll be happy, too. You say nothing scares you, but you're really frightened of everything. What can possibly happen to us?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (stammering) My love, my dear love… let me kiss your lips .I never dreamed I could still feel such tremendous emotion!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You must be more calm and more sure of yourself, now.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I am, let me kiss you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'm very tired, dear. Stay quiet and. rest yourself. Sit in the armchair.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: BERENGER, led by DAISY, sits in the armchair.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There was no point in Dudard quarrelling with Botard, as things turned out.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Don't think about Dudard any more. I'm here with you. We've no right to interfere in other people's lives.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But you're interfering in mine. You know how to be firm with me.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: That's not the same thing; I never loved Dudard.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I see what you mean. If he'd stayed he'd always have been an obstacle between us. Ah, happiness is such an egotistical thing!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You have to fight for happiness, don't you agree?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I adore you, Daisy; I admire you as well.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Maybe you won't say that when you get to know me better.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The more I know you the better you seem; and you're so beautiful, so very beautiful. (More rhinoceroses are heard passing;) Particularly compared to them ... (He points to the window.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You probably think that's no compliment, but they make you seem more beautiful than ever .. _.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Have you been. good today? You haven't had any brandy?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh yes, I've been good.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Is that the truth?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, it's the truth I assure you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Can I believe you, I wonder?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (a little flustered) Oh yes, you must believe me.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Well all right then, you can have a little glass. It'll buck you up. (BERENGER is about to leap up.) You stay where you are, dear. Where's the bottle?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (pointing,to it) There, on the little table.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: going to the table and getting the bottle and glass

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You've hidden it well away.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's out of the way of temptation..

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: pours a small glass and gives it to BERENGER

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You've been a good boy. You're making progress.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'll make a lot more now I'm with you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (handing him the glass) Here you are. That's your reward.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (downing it at one go) Thank you. (He holds up his empty glass to DAISY:)

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Oh no, dear. That's enough for this morning.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She takes his glass, puts it back on the table with the bottle.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I don't want it to make you ill. (She comes back to him.) How's your head feel now?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Much better, darling.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Then we'll take off the bandage. It doesn't suit you at all.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh no, don't touch it.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Nonsense, we'll take it off now.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm frightened there might be something underneath.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (removing the bandage in spite of his protests) Always frightened, aren't you, always imagining the worst! There's nothing there, you see. Your forehead's as smooth as a baby's.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: feeling his brow} You're right; you're·getting rid of my complexes. (DAISY kisses him on the brow.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What should I do without you?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'll never leave you alone again.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I won't have any more fears now I'm with you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'll keep them all at bay.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: We'll read books together. I'll become clever.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: And when there aren't so many people about, we'll-go for long walks.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Yes, along the Seine, and in the Luxembourg Gardens...

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: And to the Zoo.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'll be brave and strong. I'll keep you safe from harm.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You won't need to defend me, silly! We don't wish anyone any harm. And no one wishes us any, my dear.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Sometimes one does harm without meaning to, or rather one allows it to go unchecked. I know you didn't like poor old Mr. Papillon very much-but perhaps you shouldn't have spoken to him so harshly that day when Boeuf turned into a rhinoceros.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You needn't have told him he had such horny hands.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: But it was true-he had!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I know he had, my dear. But you could've said so less bluntly and not hurt his feelings so much. It had a big effect on him.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Do you think so?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: He didn't show it-he was too proud for that-but the remark certainly went home. It must have influenced his decision. Perhaps you might have been the means of saving him.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I couldn't possibly foresee what was going to happen to him ... besides he was so ill-mannered.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: For my own part, I shall never•forgive myself for not being nicer to Jean. I never managed to give him a really solid proof of the friendship I felt for him. I wasn't sufficiently understanding with him.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Don't worry about it. You did all you could. Nobody can do the impossible. There’s no point in reproaching your-self now. Stop thinking about all those people. Forget about them. You must·forget all those bad memories.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But they keep coming back to me. They're very real memories.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I never knew you were such a realist-I thought you were more poetic. Where's your imagination? There are many sides to reality. Choose the one that's best for you. Escape into the world of the imagination.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It's easy to say that!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Aren't I enough·for you?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh yes, more than enough!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You'll spoil everything if you go on having a bad conscience. Everybody has their faults, brit you and I have got less than a lot of people.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you really think so?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: We're comparatively better than most. We're good, both of us.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: That.'s true, you're good and I'm good. That's true.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Well then we have the right to live. We even owe ourselves a duty to be happy in spite of everything: Guilt is a dangerous symptom. It shows a lack of purity..

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're right, it can lead to that ...

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He points to the window under which the rhinoceroses are passing and to the up-stage wall where another rhinoceros head appears.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: ... a lot of them started like that !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: We must try and not feel guilty any more.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How right you are, my wonderful love ... You're all my happiness; the light of my life.. We are together, aren't we? No one can separate us. Our love is the only thing that's real.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Nobody has the right to stop us from being happy– in fact, nobody could, could they? (The telephone rings.) Who could that be?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (fearful) Don't answer.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Why not?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I don't know. I just feel it's better. not to.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It might be Mr. Papillon, or Botard, or Jean or Dudard ringing to say they've had second thoughts. Yon did say it was probably only a passing phase.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I don't think so. They wouldn't have changed their minds so quickly. They've not had. time to think it over. They're bound to give it a fair trial.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps·the authorities have decided to take action at last; maybe they're ringing to ask our help in whatever measures they've decided to adopt.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'd be surprised if it was them.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The telephone rings again.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It is the authorities, I tell you,I recognize the ring– a long drawn-out ring, I can't ignore an appeal from them. It can't be anyone else. (He picks up the receiver.) Hallo'? (Trumpetings are heard coming from the receiver.) You hear that?

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY puts the telephone to her ear, is shocked by the sound, quickly replaces the receiver.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (frightened) What's going on?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're playing jokes-now.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Jokes in bad taste!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You see! What did I tell you?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You didn't tell me anything.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I was expecting that; it was just what I'd predicted.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You didn't predict anything. You never do. You can only predict things after they've happened.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh yes, l can; l can predict things all right.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: That's not nice of them-in fact it's very nasty.I don't like being made fun of.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They wouldn't dare make fun of you. It's me they're making fun of.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: And naturally I come in for it as well because I'm with you. They're taking their revenge. But what have we done to them? (The telephone rings again.) Pull the plug out.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The telephone authorities say you mustn't.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Oh you never dare to do anything– and you say you could defend me !

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (darting to the radio) Let's turn on the radio for the news!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, we must find out how things stand!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The sound of trumpeting comes from the radio. BERENGER peremptorily switches it off. But in the distance other trumpetings, like echoes, can be heard.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Things are getting really serious! I tell you frankly, I don't like it! (She is trembling.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (very agitated) Keep calm ! Keep calm!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They've taken over the radio stations!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (agitated and trembling) Keep calm, keep calm!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY runs to the up-stage window, then to the down-stage window and looks out; BERENGER does the same in the opposite order, then the two come and face each other centre-stage.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It's no joke any longer. They mean business!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: There's only them left now; nobody but them. Even the authorities have joined them.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: They cross to the windows as before, and meet again centre-stage.)

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Not a soul left anywhere.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: We're all alone, we're left all alone.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: That's what you wanted.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You mean that's what you wanted!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It was you!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You! Noises come from everywhere at once. Rhinoceros heads fill the up-stage wall. From left and right in the house, the noise of rushing feet and the panting breath of the animals.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But all these disquieting sounds are nevertheless somehow rhythmical, making a kind of music. The loudest noises of all come from above; a noise of stamp-ing. Plaster falls from the ceiling. The house shakes violently.)

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: The earth's trembling! (She doesn't know where to run.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: No, that's our neighbours, the Perissodactyles !

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He shakes his fist to left and right and above.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Stop it! You're preventing us from working ! Noise is forbidden in these flats! Noise is forbidden!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They'll never listen to you! However the noise does diminish, merely forming a sort of musical background.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (he, too, is afraid) Don't be frightened, my dear. We're together– you're happy with me, aren't you? It's enough that I'm with you, isn't it? I'll chase all your fears away.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Perhaps it's all our own fault.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Don't think about it any longer. We mustn't start feeling remorse. It's dangerous to start feeling guilty. We must just live our lives, and be happy. We have the right to be happy. They're not spiteful, and we're not doing them any harm.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They'll leave·us in peace. You just keep calm and rest. Sit in the armchair. (He leads her to the armchair.) Just keep calm! (DAISY sits in the armchair.) Would you like a drop of brandy to pull you together?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I've got a headache.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (taking up his bandage and binding DAISY'S head) I love you, my darling. Don't you worry, they'll get over it. It's-just a passing phase.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They won't get over it. It's for good.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I love you. I love you madly.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (taking off the bandage) Let things just take their course. 'What can we do about it?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They've all gone mad. The world is sick. They're all sick.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: We shan't be the ones to cure them.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How can we live in the same house with them?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: ' (calming down) We must be sensible. We must adapt ourselves and try and get along with them.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They can't understand us.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They must. There's no other way.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you understand them? .

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Not yet. But we must try to understand the way their minds work, and learn their language.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They haven't got a language! Listen ... do you call that a language?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: How do you know? You're no polyglot17!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: We'll talk about it later. We must have lunch first.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I'm not hungry any more. It's all too much. I can't take any more.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: But you're the strong one. You're not going to let it get you down. It's precisely for your courage that I admire you so.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You said that before.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Do you feel sure of my love?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Yes, of course.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I love you so.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You keep saying the same thing, my dear.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Listen, Daisy, there is something we can do. We'll have children, and our children will have children-it'll take time, but together we can regenerate the human race.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Regenerate.the human race?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: It happened once before.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Ages ago.· Adam and Eve ... They had a lot of courage.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: And we, too, can have courage. We don't need all that much. It happens automatically with time and patience.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: What's the use?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Of course we can– with a little bit of courage.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I don't want to have children– it's a bore.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: How can we save the world, if you don't?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Why bother to save it?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What a thing to say! Do it for me, Daisy. Let's save the world.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: After all, perhaps it's we who need saving. Perhaps we're the abnormal ones. ,.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You're not yourself, Daisy, you've got a touch of fever.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: There aren't any more of our kind about anywhere, are there?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Daisy, you're not to talk like that!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: DAISY looks all around,at the rhinoceros heads on the walls, on the landing ·door, and now starting to appear along the footlights.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Those are the real people. They look happy. They're content to be what they are. They don't look insane. They look very natural. They were right to do what they did.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (clasping his hands and looking despairingly at DAISY) We're the ones who are doing right, Daisy, I assure you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: That's very presumptuous of you!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: :You know perfectly well I'm right.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: There's no such thing as absolute right. It's the world that's right– not you and me.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I am right, Daisy. And the proof is that you understand me when I speak to you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: What does that prove?

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The proof is that I love you as much as it's possible for a man to love a woman.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Funny sort of argument!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I don't understand you any longer; Daisy. You don't know what you're saying, darling. Think of our love! Our love...

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I feel a bit ashamed of what you call love– this morbid feeling, this male weakness. And female, too. It just doesn't compare with the ardour and the tremendous energy emanating from all these creatures around us.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Energy! You want some energy, do you? I can let you have some energy! (He slaps her face,)

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Oh! I never would have believed it possible… (She sinks into the armchair.)

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh forgive me, my darling, please forgive me! (He tries to embrace her, she evades him.) Forgive me, my darling. I didn't mean it. I don't know what came over me, losing control like that !

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It's because you've run out of arguments, that's why.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Oh dear! In the space of a few minutes we've gone through twenty-five years of married life.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I pity you. I understand you all too well ...

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (as DAISY weeps) You're probably right that I've run out of arguments. You think they’re stronger than me, stronger than us. Maybe they are.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Indeed they are.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well, in spite of everything, l swear to you I'll never give in, never!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: she rises, goes to BERENGER, puts her arms round his neck

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: My poor darling, I'll help you to resist– to the very end.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Will you be capable of it?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: I give you my word. You can trust me.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: The rhinoceros noises have become melodious.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Listen, they're singing !

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're not singing, they're roaring.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They're singing.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're roaring, I tell you.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You're mad, they're singing.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You can't have a very musical ear, then.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You don't know the first thing about music– and look, they're dancing!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You call that dancing?

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: It's their way of dancing... They're beautiful.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're disgusting!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You're not to say unpleasant things about them. It upsets me.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm sorry. We're not going to quarrel on their account.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: They're like gods.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: You go too far, Daisy! Take a good look at them.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: You mustn't be jealous my dear.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She goes to BERENGER again and tries to embrace him..This time it is BERENGER who frees himself.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I can see our opinions are directly opposed. It's better not to discuss the matter.

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: Now you mustn't be nasty.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Then don't you be stupid!

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: (to BERENGER, who·turns his back on her. He looks at himself closely in the mirror) It's no longer possible for us to live together.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: As BERENGER continues to examine himself in the mirror she goes quietly to the door, saying:

script.speaker: Daisy
script.text: He isn't very nice, really, he isn't very nice.

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: She goes out, and is seen slowly descending the stairs.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (still looking at himself in the mirror) Men aren't so bad-looking, you know. And I'm not a particularly handsome specimen! Believe me, Daisy! (He turns round.) Daisy! Daisy! Where are you, Daisy? You can't do that to me! (He darts to the door.) Daisy!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He gets to the landing and leans over the banister.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: . Daisy ! Come back! Come back, my dear ! You haven't even had your lunch .Daisy, don't leave me alone! Remember your promise! Daisy! Daisy!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He stops calling, makes a despairing gesture, and comes back into the room.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Well, it was obvious we weren't getting along together. It just wasn't working out. But she shouldn't have left like that with no explanation. (He looks all around:) She didn't even leave a note. That's no way to behave. Now I'm all on my own.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: (He locks the door carefully, but angrily.) But they won't get me. (He carefully closes the windows.) You won't get me!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He addresses all the rhinoceros heads.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm not joining you; I don't understand you! I'm staying as I am. I'm a human being. A human being. (He sits in the armchair.) It's my fault she's gone. What'll become of her? I can easily picture the worst, because the worst can easily happen.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Poor little thing left all alone in this world of monsters! Nobody can help me find her, nobody, because there's nobody left. Fresh trumpetings, hectic racings, clouds of dust.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I can't bear the sound of them any longer

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He plugs his ears, and talks to.himself in the mirror.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: The only solution is to convince them– but convince them of what? Are the changes reversible, that's the main issue. Are they reversible? In any case, to convince them you'd have to talk to them. And to talk to them I'd have to learn their language.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Or they'd have to learn mine. But what language do I speak? What is my language? Am I speaking English? Yes, it must be English. But what is English? I can call it English if I want, and nobody can say it isn't-I'm the only one who speaks it.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: What am I saying? Do I understand what I'm saying? Do I? (He crosses to the middle of the room.) And what if it's true what Daisy said, and they're the ones in the right? (He turns back to the mirror.) A man's not ugly to look at, not ugly at all!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He examines himself, passing his hand over his face.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm not good-looking, I'm not good-looking. He takes down the pictures, throws them furiously to the ground, and goes over to the mirror.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: They're the good-looking ones: I was wrong! Oh, how I wish I was like them! I haven't got any horns, more's the pity ! A smooth brow looks so ugly. I need one or two horns to give my sagging face a lift.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: Perhaps one will grow and I needn't be ashamed any more-then I could go and join them. But it will never grow! (He· looks at the palms of his hands.) My hands are so limp-oh, why won't they get rough!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He takes his coat off, undoes his shirt to look at his chest in the mirror.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I can't stand this white, hairy body. Oh I'd love to have a hard skin in that wonderful dull green colour-a skin without any hair on it, like theirs! (He listens to the trumpetings.) Their song is charming– a bit raucous perhaps, but it does have charm!

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I wishI could do it! (He tries to imitate them.) Ahh, Ahh, Brr! No, that's not it! Try again, louder! Ahh, Ahh, Brr! No, that's not it,·it's too feeble, it's got no drive behind it. Ahh, Ahh, Brr. I'm not trumpeting at all! I'm just howling.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I've only myself to blame; I should have gone with them while there was still time. Now it's too late! Now I'm a monster, just a monster. Now I'll never become a rhinoceros, I’ll ever, never! I've gone past changing.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I want to, I really do, but I can't, I just can't. I can't stand the sight of me. I'm too ashamed! I'm so ugly!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: He turns his back on the mirror.

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: People who try to hang on to their individuality always come to a bad end! (He suddenly snaps out of it.) Oh well, too bad ! I'll take on the whole of them! I'll put up a fight against the lot of them, the whole lot of them !

script.speaker: Berenger
script.text: I'm the last man left, and I'm staying that way until the end. I'm not capitulating!

script.speaker: Stage
script.text: THE END
